newsitem.title: CANADA: HORSE RACING-CIGAR OFF TO STUD AS ACCOLADES POUR IN.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-CIGAR OFF TO STUD AS ACCOLADES POUR IN.

text.p: The world of thoroughbred racing usually throws around accolades for opponents like they were anvils, but once again, as was the case throughout his magnificent career, Cigar is the exception.
"He's the best horse in the world and we beat him," said Alphabet Soup trainer David Hofmans after his horse scored an upset win over the great Cigar in the Breeders' Cup Classic on Saturday.
"He ran great, but he's at the end of a long, hard year. There's nothing to take away from him," Hofmans said of Cigar.

The international superstar finished third in his final race after a very game, but under-powered effort that provided a clear view for 41,250 fans at Woodbine Racetrack of just how age has leeched the once awesome talent from the six year old.
In his prime, Cigar would not have been fazed by having to go wide at the top of the stretch and needing a big final kick to win.

Saturday, he was ready to make his customary move down the stretch coming from far outside and jockey Jerry Bailey, who won this race aboard Cigar last year, asked the horse for some extra burn. This time it just wasn't there.
Instead there was six years and the residue of a hard life at the races and a respectable third place.
Chris McCarren, who kept Alphabet Soup in front long enough to beat Louis Quatorze by a nose, paid tribute to his own mount, saying he had a "heart as big as the track."
Then going against the thoroughbred racing norm, he also heaped praise on Cigar.
"I feel fortunate to be on the right horse to beat him when he was beatable," McCarron said.

"To possibly take something away from Cigar doesn't really sit very well with me because I have the utmost respect for Cigar, as does everyone in this room," McCarron said of the horse who won 17 of his last 20 races, including a storied 16 consecutive victories that tied the legendary Citation before the string was broken in August.
Cigar's trainer, Bill Mott, acknowledged the ageing process had taken its toll in Cigar's missing outside drive.
"When he was at his very, very, very best, he would shoot by and open up. Maybe he's lost a step," Mott said.
"He's been wearing them down his last few races, not shooting by. Probably he shows the evidence of four years of racing, hard racing, and a lot of travel," added Mott.
"I'm not torn apart (by the loss)," Mott said. "When Jerry (Bailey) got off and we walked back, my feeling was more of appreciation than any type of letdown for the loss.
"If you want to be realistic, you know that it just can't go on. It just can't. It wouldn't be possible. He's just flesh and blood and he's wearing down."
Added Hofmans, who may be remembered as the man who trained the last horse to beat Cigar: "If there is a chink in his armour, it's because he ran long and hard all year long.
"I don't know if there'll ever be another Cigar."
But as the accolades and melancholy farewells pour in, Cigar may be smiling at the thought of his next career as a stud in which he will try to prove Hofmans wrong.
